Kabaddi Raid

3D kabaddi for your phone · Raid, touch and race home

  • 7 v 7

Kabaddi Raid is a 3D kabaddi game for your phone. Cross the baulk line on one breath, touch a defender and race back over the midline before they bring you down.

Or defend: read the raid, take him by the ankle, the thigh or the waist, and chain up with a team-mate.

Join the beta

Features

Three ways to play

Quick Match, a League Season with your own franchise and the player auction, and the Nations Cup.

Raid and tackle

Hand and toe touches, kicks, the dubki and the lion jump; ankle, thigh and waist holds and chain tackles.

The rules as played

Bonus points, revivals, all outs, do-or-die raids, super tackles and the golden raid, with referees signalling every call.

Breath or the clock

Raid on one breath of the cant, or against the 30-second clock: your choice.

Five grounds

Twelve franchises, twelve countries and five grounds, from a village mat to a stadium under lights.

Controls your way

A stick wherever your thumb lands, a left-handed layout, movable buttons and four levels from Rookie to Legend.

About the sport

Kabaddi is a contact team sport from South Asia, played seven a side. A raider crosses into the other half, touches as many defenders as he can and must get back over the midline before they bring him down, either on one breath while chanting the cant or against a 30-second clock. Defenders score by stopping him: ankle holds, thigh holds, chain tackles.

pages.title: Kabaddi Raid privacy policy
pages.content:
The same policy is in the game: Settings > About > Privacy policy. Questions about the game itself: Kabaddi Raid help.

Last updated 27 October 2026. Kabaddi Raid is a kabaddi game for Android phones and tablets, made by Josh Nason.

In short

Kabaddi Raid does not collect, send, share or sell any personal data. There is no account, no advertising, no analytics and no tracking. The Android app does not have permission to use the internet: everything you do in the game stays on your phone.

What the game keeps, and where

In its own private storage on your phone, and nowhere else: your settings (language, sound and volume, vibration, graphics, camera, controls, difficulty) and your saved games (your League Season and your Nations Cup). Other apps cannot read them, they are not sent anywhere, and they are not part of your phone's cloud backup. Uninstalling the game deletes them; updating it keeps them.

Permissions

The game asks for one permission: vibration, so the phone can buzz at a tackle or a point (you can turn it off in Settings). It does not ask to use the internet, your location, contacts, camera, microphone, photos or files. Everything the game shows, these pages included, comes with it.

Links

A few buttons (View online on this page and on Help) open a page in your phone's web browser. The game sends nothing when you tap one; the page is covered by the policy of the site it is on.

The browser version

A version of the game also runs in a web browser, at kabaddi-raid-beta.netlify.app. That page is served by Netlify, which keeps standard server logs (such as your IP address and browser type) under Netlify's privacy policy. The game sends nothing to us there either; its settings and saved games stay in your browser's storage on your device.

Children

Kabaddi Raid is a sports game for players of all ages. It collects no personal information from anyone, children included.

Changes

If this policy changes, the new version comes with the game and is posted online, with a new date. If the game ever starts to collect any data, the policy will say so before the update that does it is released.

Contact

Questions about this policy or the game: https://thekabaddipulse.com/contact/

pages.title: Kabaddi Raid help and support
pages.content:
Help for Kabaddi Raid. The same help is in the game: Settings > About > Help.

Something not working, or an idea for the game? Tell us through our contact page, with your phone's model and what happened. A screenshot helps.

Playing

How do I raid?

Move with the stick on the left of the screen (put your thumb down anywhere there). Cross the baulk line, touch a defender with Hand touch or Kick, then get back over the midline before your breath (or the raid clock) runs out. Dodge, Dubki and Lion jump get you out of a tackle; if you are caught, Break free lights up. How to Play, on the home screen, goes through every move and rule.

How do I defend?

You control one defender (tap another player to switch). Hold the raider with Ankle, Thigh or Waist, or Dash him out of the court. Chain links you with a team-mate for a chain tackle.

What are the modes?

  • Quick Match: two teams, one ground, play now.
  • League Season: own a franchise. Keep your best players, win the auction, then the league and the final, season after season.
  • Nations Cup: pick a country and its squad of twelve, through the groups to the final.

How do I change the language?

Tap the language button on the home screen. The game speaks English, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Bengali and Punjabi, and starts in your phone's language if it is one of them.

Your phone

The game is slow or jerky

Open Settings and set Graphics to Medium or Low. The game also lowers it by itself if your phone cannot keep up, and says so on screen.

Will I lose my season if I update?

No. Updates keep your settings and saved games. Uninstalling the game deletes them, because they are kept only on your phone (see the privacy policy).

Measuring a problem for us

Tap the version number on the home screen seven times to turn on the developer's overlay. Play until the problem happens, tap Copy summary and paste it into your message. Seven more taps turn it off.

Is there an iPhone version?

Not yet. The browser version, at kabaddi-raid-beta.netlify.app, plays on an iPhone, iPad or computer: turn a phone sideways, and tap once to start the sound.

Through our contact page: thekabaddipulse.com/contact.

pages.title: Hurling Heroes help and support
pages.content:
Help for Hurling Heroes. The same help is in the game: Settings > About > Help.

Playing

  • Your player has the gold ring. Your left thumb anywhere on the left of the screen runs him; the buttons on the right are what he can do now. SWITCH changes him to the teammate best placed for the ball.
  • With the sliotar: STRIKE shoots for a point (or, with the joystick pushed another way, strikes a long ball to the teammate there); GOAL, close in, drives it low for the net; PASS hand-passes it; SOLO puts it on your hurley before your four steps are up (the dots over your player count them), and HAND takes it back, your second and last catch.
  • Without it: CATCH or LIFT it when it comes near, PULL to strike it first time; near the man on the ball, TACKLE, and BLOCK when he goes to strike.
  • Restarts: your puck-out LONG or SHORT; your free, 65 or sideline cut STRIKE at the posts or PASS; a penalty, aim and GOAL.
  • Too much to manage? Settings > Help with the ball > Full: your player solos by himself and runs for loose balls when your thumb is off the joystick.

The rules

The game plays the playing rules of hurling in force in 2026: two halves of 35 minutes (30 at club level), a goal worth three points, four steps and two catches, the 13-metre and 20-metre rules at restarts, yellow and red cards, the black card and sin bin for denying a goal chance, extra time and penalties in knock-out games. How to Play in the game has the whole of it.

If something is wrong

  • The game runs slowly or the phone gets warm: Settings > Graphics > Low, and Frame rate > Battery saver. Phones with less memory start on Low by themselves.
  • The beta will not install on an older or Android Go phone: use the file ending in -32bit.apk from the beta page.
  • The Irish looks wrong (an bhfuil an Ghaeilge mícheart?): please tell us which screen and what it says; we want it right.
  • The buttons are hard to reach: Settings > Button size, Move buttons to drag them where you want them, and Left-handed to swap the sides.

Playing

pages.title: Netball Unleashed help and support
pages.content:
Help for Netball Unleashed. The same help is in the game: Settings > About > Help.

Playing

  • Your player has the lime ring at her feet. The joystick (your left thumb, anywhere on the left of the screen) runs her. Lead into space to get free for a pass.
  • With the ball she may not run: that is footwork. Push the joystick toward a team-mate to pick her (a ring shows who), then Pass, or Lob over a defender. The ring over the ball is your three seconds.
  • Shooting: Shoot appears when your Goal Shooter or Goal Attack has the ball in the circle.
  • Defending: Defend puts her arms up. Keep 0.9 m from the landing foot of the player with the ball (the ring round it turns red when you are closer) or the umpire calls obstruction. Intercept leaps for a pass.

pages.title: Kabaddi
pages.content:
What is kabaddi?

Kabaddi is a team contact sport from South Asia. Two teams of seven take turns to attack and defend on a small court split in half by a midline.

The attacker is called the raider. One raider at a time crosses into the other half, tries to touch as many defenders as possible, and then has to get back over the midline. The defenders try to stop that by tackling and holding the raider.

It needs no ball and no equipment, just a flat court, so it has long been played in villages and school yards. Today it is also a fast, televised professional sport, led by India's Pro Kabaddi League.

History and origins

Ancient roots and tradition

Kabaddi almost certainly began on the Indian subcontinent, but nobody can date it precisely. Wikipedia's article, citing historians such as Ronojoy Sen, says it probably goes back thousands of years, possibly to the Vedic period.

Some stories are tradition rather than proven history. A popular one compares kabaddi to the Mahabharata episode in which the young warrior Abhimanyu enters the Kauravas' chakravyuha (a circular battle formation) and is trapped inside it, much like a raider surrounded by defenders. This is a comparison, not evidence that the epic describes kabaddi. Tales that Krishna or the Buddha played an early form of the game are also traditions. Other accounts place the game's origin in ancient Tamilakam (South India) or in Persia.

Even the name is debated. An often-quoted explanation links "kabaddi" to Tamil words meaning "holding hands", but scholars such as the anthropologist Joseph Alter say the word's origin is unclear.

Many local names

The same basic game has many regional names, for example:

  • hu-tu-tu in western India
  • chedugudu in Andhra Pradesh
  • ha-du-du (hadudu) in Bengal and Bangladesh
  • sadugudu in Tamil Nadu
  • gudu in Sri Lanka and bhavatik in the Maldives

Traditional forms

Before the modern rules, many local versions existed. The best known today is circle style, also called Punjabi kabaddi. It is played on a round pitch about 22 m across, with one raider against one defender at a time, and players are not sent off the field.

Other older Indian forms include Sanjeevani, where a player who is out can be revived, and Gaminee, where out players stay out until the whole side is out. Beach kabaddi and indoor versions with smaller teams are also played.

The modern game

Modern rules for the rectangular "standard" game were written in Maharashtra in 1921, revised in 1923, and used at a national tournament in Baroda that year. Kabaddi was shown at the 1936 Berlin Olympics as a demonstration sport.

National organisation followed: the All India Kabaddi Federation was set up in 1950, and the Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI) in 1972. Kabaddi also became Bangladesh's national sport in 1972. The first Asian Kabaddi Championship was held in 1980, and kabaddi became an Asian Games medal sport in 1990.

How it's played

These are the standard-style rules used in international events such as the Asian Games. Professional leagues add their own twists, and details change between editions and seasons.

The court

The court is a rectangle, about 13 m by 10 m for men and 12 m by 8 m for women (smaller for juniors). A midline divides it into two halves.

In each half there are two more lines parallel to the midline:

  • The baulk line, 3.75 m from the midline for men (3 m for women). A raider must cross it for the raid to count.
  • The bonus line, 1 m beyond the baulk line, used for bonus points.

Along the two long sides are 1 m strips called the lobbies. Around the whole court there is a clear safety area of about 4 m.

Teams and positions

Each team has seven players on court and a few substitutes. Players are usually described as:

  • Raiders, who attack.
  • Defenders, often split into corners (at the two ends of the defensive line) and covers (in the middle).
  • All-rounders, who both raid and defend.

The raid

Teams take turns sending in one raider. The raider must cross the midline and the baulk line, try to touch defenders with a hand or foot, and return to their own half.

Traditionally there was no clock: the raid lasted only as long as one breath. To prove they were not breathing in, raiders keep chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi..." without pause. This chant is called the cant. Stopping the cant in the opponents' half is a technical foul.

Modern rules add a 30-second limit on each raid. This came in with the Pro Kabaddi League in 2014, and the 30-second clock is now the main time limit in the standard game. Rule summaries still describe the cant as well, so the two exist side by side.

Scoring

  • Touch points: the raider scores one point for every defender touched, if the raider gets back to their own half. Those defenders are out.
  • Tackle point: if the defenders stop the raider getting home, the defending side scores a point and the raider is out.
  • Bonus point: if six or more defenders are on court, a raider can earn a bonus point by reaching the bonus line with one foot while the other foot is in the air.
  • All out: if a team puts all seven opponents out, it scores two extra points and the whole opposing team comes back on.
  • Revival: when a team scores a point, one of its out players comes back, in the order they went out. Bonus points and technical points do not revive players.

A player who steps out of bounds during a raid is out. A raider who fails to cross the baulk line without touching anyone is also out.

Professional league extras

The Pro Kabaddi League uses extra rules and terms:

  • Do-or-die raid: after two empty raids in a row, the team's next raider must score or is out.
  • Super raid: a raid worth three or more points.
  • Super tackle: a tackle by a team with three or fewer defenders left on court; it earns an extra point.

The lobby rules have also changed over time. ESPN reported that from Season 9 (2022) a defender who follows a raider into the lobby is no longer ruled out.

Fouls and cards

Misconduct is dealt with by cards:

  • A green card is a warning.
  • A yellow card suspends a player for two minutes.
  • A red card sends a player off, possibly for the rest of the tournament.

Officials

A standard match has a referee, two umpires, a scorer and two assistant scorers. The referee handles the coin toss, the time and substitutions; the umpires watch the lines and contacts.

Match length

A match has two halves, each 20 minutes for men and 15 minutes for women, with a five-minute break. Teams change ends at half time.

If a match that needs a winner ends level, each team makes five raids with five different raiders. If it is still tied, a coin toss decides who takes a golden raid, and the first team to score wins.

Equipment

Kabaddi needs very little:

  • A flat, soft court. Top-level games use synthetic mats; village games are often on earth.
  • Shorts or a sports kit with numbered shirts.
  • Light, grippy shoes, or bare feet in traditional matches.

There is no ball, stick or protective gear.

Where it's played today

Governing bodies

  • The International Kabaddi Federation (IKF) was formed in 2004 as the first worldwide governing body.
  • The Asian Kabaddi Federation runs the sport in Asia and is linked to the Olympic Council of Asia.
  • The Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI), formed in 1972, runs the sport in India.
  • World Kabaddi, founded in 2018, runs a separate international circuit. Circle-style events are organised by other bodies.

Asian Games

Kabaddi was a demonstration event in 1951 and 1982 and became a medal sport in 1990. India won the men's gold at every Games from 1990 to 2014.

In 2018, Iran won both the men's and women's titles. India took both golds back at the 2022 Games in Hangzhou (held in 2023), beating Iran 33–29 in the men's final. At the 2026 Games in Aichi–Nagoya, India beat Iran in both finals again: 40–34 for the men and 37–34 for the women.

World Cups

The IKF's standard-style Kabaddi World Cup has been held in 2004 (Mumbai), 2007 (Panvel) and 2016 (Ahmedabad). India won all three, beating Iran in each final. Women's editions were held in 2012 (Patna) and 2025 (Dhaka), both won by India.

A separate circle-style Kabaddi World Cup was mostly held in Punjab, India, from 2010. India won every men's edition until 2020, when Pakistan won at home.

Pro Kabaddi League

The Pro Kabaddi League (PKL) began in 2014 with eight teams and grew to 12. It is shown on Star Sports. Jaipur Pink Panthers won the first season, beating U Mumba 35–24.

Patna Pirates have won the most titles, three in a row (two seasons in 2016, then 2017). Dabang Delhi K.C. won the 2025 season, beating Puneri Paltan 31–28 in the final.

Other leagues have followed, such as Pakistan's one-off Super Kabaddi League (2018) and the Nepal Kabaddi League (first held in 2025). Europe has had its own championship since 2019.

Famous moments and players

  • Pardeep Narwal's 34 points (2017). In a Season 5 eliminator in Mumbai on 23 October 2017, Narwal scored 34 raid points as Patna Pirates beat Haryana Steelers 69–30, then a league record. The official report also notes one super raid that put out six Haryana players. Nicknamed the "Dubki King", he won three straight PKL titles with Patna and retired in 2025. (Source: Pro Kabaddi; Wikipedia.)
  • Pawan Sehrawat's 39 points (2019). In Season 7, Sehrawat scored 39 raid points for Bengaluru Bulls in a 59–36 win over Haryana Steelers, breaking Narwal's record and outscoring the whole opposing team. (Source: Pro Kabaddi.)
  • Anup Kumar. Known as "Captain Cool", he won Asian Games gold in 2010 and 2014, captained India to the 2016 World Cup title and led U Mumba to the 2015 PKL title. He received the Arjuna Award in 2012 and retired in 2018. (Source: Wikipedia.)

pages.title: Hurling
pages.content:
What is hurling?

Hurling is an Irish field game for two teams of 15. Players use a wooden stick called a hurley (camán in Irish) to strike a small leather ball called a sliotar.

You can hit the ball on the ground or in the air, catch it in your hand, and run with it balanced on the hurley. Strikes are fast: a well-hit sliotar can travel more than 110 m.

Teams score by sending the ball over the crossbar for a point or under it into the net for a goal, worth three points. The game is run by the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA). Its players are amateurs, including at the top level.

In 2018 UNESCO added hurling to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The listing also covers camogie, the women's game.

History and origins

Ancient roots, legend and evidence

Hurling is very old, but its exact age is debated. UNESCO describes it as dating back about 2,000 years. Some writers claim three thousand years or more, but that figure rests on mythology, not evidence.

Legend: Irish mythological texts place a hurling game at the Battle of Moytura (Cath Maige Tuired). The best-known legend is in the Táin cycle. In it the boy hero Cúchulainn (Cú Chulainn) plays hurling at Emain Macha. These are stories, not historical records.

Written evidence: Early Irish (Brehon) law texts mention the game. Commentaries on the Seanchas Mór say a king's son could have a hurley hooped with bronze, while other boys had copper. Another law tract, Meallbretha, deals with compensation for injuries in games, most of them like hurling.

Physical evidence: The earliest archaeological finds of hurling balls date from the later 12th century.

Bans, gentry matches and a new association

Colonial authorities tried more than once to restrict the game. The Statute of Kilkenny (1366) banned "horlinge" among the English settlers. A 1527 statute in Galway also restricted the "little ball" game played with hooked sticks.

The 18th century is often called hurling's golden age. Landowners organised big matches between parishes and counties. Two styles existed: a northern winter game (camán), where you could not handle the ball, and a southern summer game (iomán or báire), where you could.

The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded on 1 November 1884 in Hayes' Hotel, Thurles, County Tipperary. Michael Cusack, one of its founders, wrote modern rules based mainly on the southern game.

The first All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship was played in 1887. Its final was played on 1 April 1888 in Birr. Thurles, representing Tipperary, won it.

Sister games

Camogie is the women's version of hurling. Its first matches were played in 1904 and its association was founded in 1905. Its rules are similar, with some differences, such as 60-minute games and a smaller sliotar.

Scotland's shinty is a close cousin of hurling. Since 1896, Ireland and Scotland have played international matches under a mix of the two codes' rules.

How it's played

The rules below follow the GAA Official Guide Part 2, effective from 10 March 2025, plus changes voted on in 2026 (noted where they apply).

The pitch

Hurling is played on a grass pitch 130–145 m long and 80–90 m wide. Gaelic football uses the same pitch.

  • Lines cross the pitch at 13 m, 20 m, 45 m and 65 m from each end line. The 65 m line is used only in hurling. A short halfway line is marked in the centre.
  • Arc: A semicircle with a 13 m radius sits outside each 20 m line. In football there is also a 40 m arc, but that arc is for football only.
  • Goals: H-shaped posts 6.5 m apart, at least 7 m tall, with a crossbar 2.5 m above the ground and a net below it.
  • Rectangles: A small rectangle (14 m × 4.5 m) and a large rectangle (19 m × 13 m) are marked in front of each goal.

Teams and positions

Each team has 15 players: a goalkeeper and 14 outfield players. The traditional line-up is:

  • Goalkeeper
  • Full-back line: right corner-back, full-back, left corner-back
  • Half-back line: right wing-back, centre-back, left wing-back
  • Midfield: two midfielders
  • Half-forward line: right wing-forward, centre-forward, left wing-forward
  • Full-forward line: right corner-forward, full-forward, left corner-forward

A team may use five substitutes in normal time, plus extra substitutes for blood injuries or suspected head injuries.

Scoring

  • Point: over the crossbar between the posts. Worth 1.
  • Goal: under the crossbar into the net. Worth 3.

Scores are written as goals–points. For example, 1-29 means one goal and 29 points, a total of 32.

You may not throw the ball in for a score or carry it over the goal line. You may strike the ball in flight with your hand.

Two-point scores are for Gaelic football, not hurling. From 2025 the GAA trialled a two-point score from outside a 40 m arc in football. At a Special Congress in October 2025 that rule became permanent from 1 January 2026. In the hurling rules, a point is still worth one, wherever it is struck from.

Key rules

  • Lifting: You may not pick the ball off the ground with your hand. Lift it with the hurley, or flick it up with your foot.
  • Carrying: You may hold the ball in your hand for no more than four steps. To go further, balance or bounce it on the hurley (a "solo"). After catching the ball, you can bring it back into your hand only once.
  • Handpass: You may pass with the hand, but only with a clear striking action. Throwing the ball is a foul.
  • Shoulder charge: This is allowed shoulder to shoulder, with at least one foot on the ground, against a player who has or is playing the ball.
  • Goalkeeper: Inside the small rectangle the goalkeeper may not be charged.
  • Restarts: After a score or a wide, the goalkeeper restarts with a puck-out from the small rectangle. If a defender sends the ball wide, the attackers get a free from the 65 m line. If the ball goes out over the sideline, the other team takes a sideline cut from the ground.

Fouls and cards

Technical fouls, such as over-carrying, throwing the ball or picking it off the ground, give the other team a free puck. Defenders must stand 20 m back for a free.

Aggressive fouls, such as tripping, pulling down or careless use of the hurley, lead to a free and a yellow card. Two cautions mean a red card, and the player is sent off. Striking or kicking an opponent with force is a straight red.

Penalty puck: An aggressive foul by a defender inside the large rectangle gives a penalty. It is struck from the centre of the 20 m line, and only one defender (usually the goalkeeper) may stand on the goal line. This one-defender rule dates from 2015.

Black card (cynical fouls): In inter-county senior, under-20 and minor games, there is an extra rule. If a player pulls down, trips or recklessly hurls an attacker who has a goal-scoring chance, the attacking team gets a penalty. The offender gets a black card and 10 minutes in the sin bin. Congress first approved this sin-bin rule for hurling on a trial basis in 2021.

Dissent: The 2025 rulebook moved a free 13 m forward when a player showed dissent. At its February 2026 Congress, the GAA voted to bring hurling into line with football's dissent rules. A free can now be moved 30 m forward (it is 50 m in football).

Officials

A senior match has a referee, two linesmen and four umpires, two at each goal. Inter-county senior games add a sideline official, who handles substitutions.

The umpires signal scores with flags: green for a goal and white for a point. They cross their arms above their heads for a wide. At Croke Park and some other approved grounds, the Hawk-Eye system can check whether a ball went over the bar or wide.

Match length

  • Inter-county senior championship and league games: 70 minutes, in two halves of 35.
  • Most other games: 60 minutes, in two halves of 30. Younger grades can be shorter.
  • Extra time: two periods of 10 minutes. Drawn knockout games then go to a "winner on the day" method set by the GAA.

Rules being trialled

In September 2026 the GAA's Hurling Expert Advisory Group recommended 24 rule changes. They will be tested in third-level (Higher Education) league games from October 2026.

The proposals include six steps instead of four, no handpass straight after another handpass, and two points for a sideline cut struck over the bar. These are trials only. They are not part of the standard rules unless the GAA adopts them later.

Equipment

  • Hurley (camán): A curved wooden stick, usually made of ash. Hurleys are typically about 61–91 cm (24–36 in) long, chosen to suit the player's height. The flat, wide end is called the bas. A goalkeeper's bas is much bigger. Metal bands on the bas must be taped over in games up to under-12.
  • Sliotar: A cork-centred ball with a leather cover and a raised rib. It must be 69–72 mm across and weigh 110–116 g, and match balls carry a GAA mark of approval. White was traditional, and yellow balls are now widely used. The rules also allow a smart chip in the sliotar to show it is genuine.
  • Helmet: A helmet with a face guard is compulsory in all hurling games and training. The rule has applied to all grades since 1 January 2010 (minor and under-21 grades began in 2009). Helmets must meet the Irish standard IS:355 and must not be altered.
  • Kit: County or club jersey, shorts and socks. The goalkeeper wears a different-coloured jersey.

Where it's played today

The GAA governs hurling worldwide from Croke Park in Dublin. Clubs exist across Ireland and in Britain, North America, Europe, Australia and Asia.

  • All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship: The top inter-county competition. The winners lift the Liam MacCarthy Cup, first presented in 1923. Liam MacCarthy was a London-born son of Irish parents who helped found the London GAA board. Croke Park has hosted almost every final since 1910.
  • Provincial championships: Notably Munster and Leinster.
  • National Hurling League: The spring inter-county league.
  • Club championships: County titles lead to the All-Ireland Club Championship.
  • Camogie: The Camogie Association runs the women's game. Its All-Ireland winners receive the O'Duffy Cup.

After the 2026 final, Kilkenny still lead the roll of honour with 36 All-Ireland senior titles. Cork have 30, Tipperary 29 (including 2025) and Limerick 13 (including 2026).

Famous moments and players

  • Christy Ring (Cork, 1920–1979): Won eight All-Ireland senior medals with Cork and 18 Railway Cup medals with Munster. He is often named among the greatest hurlers. Source: Christy Ring - Wikipedia.
  • Henry Shefflin (Kilkenny): Won 10 All-Ireland senior medals, more than any other player, along with 11 All Stars. He is the only three-time Hurler of the Year (2002, 2006, 2012). Source: Henry Shefflin - Wikipedia.
  • Kilkenny's four in a row (2006–2009): Kilkenny won four finals in a row. They beat Cork, Limerick, Waterford and Tipperary. Source: List of All-Ireland SHC finals.
  • Limerick's modern era: Limerick won four finals in a row from 2020 to 2023 and added another in 2026, beating Galway 1-29 to 1-18. Source: List of All-Ireland SHC finals.
  • London, 1901: London is the only team from outside Ireland to win the All-Ireland senior title. Source: Hurling - Wikipedia.
  • An Olympic cameo, 1904: Hurling was a demonstration sport at the St. Louis Olympics. Innisfails of St. Louis beat the Fenians of Chicago. Source: Hurling - Wikipedia.

pages.title: Sepak takraw
pages.content:
What is sepak takraw?

Sepak takraw is often called "kick volleyball". Two teams face each other across a net on a court the size of a badminton doubles court. They keep a light woven ball in the air and send it over the net using their feet, knees, chest and head, but never their hands or arms.

Each side may touch the ball up to three times before it must go over. A point is won when the ball lands in the opponent's court or the other team makes a fault.

The headline move is the spike. The attacker leaps, flips backwards or sideways and kicks the ball down over the net with the foot higher than the head. It is one of the most acrobatic sights in any sport.

The sport is hugely popular in Southeast Asia, above all in Thailand and Malaysia, and is now played in dozens of countries.

History and origins

An old game of keeping the ball up

Long before there was a net, people across Southeast Asia played circle games of keeping a woven rattan ball in the air without using their hands. The game had many local names:

  • Sepak raga in Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and Indonesia.
  • Takraw in Thailand, with a related game in Laos.
  • Sipa in the Philippines, a traditional game that is related to sepak takraw and has its own over-the-net forms.
  • Chinlone in Myanmar. This is a separate, mostly non-competitive game: a team of about six players passes the ball around a circle, judged on skill and style rather than beating an opponent.

How old these games are is hard to pin down. The Malay Annals describe a rattan-ball game in the 15th-century Malacca Sultanate, and Thai records place it in the reign of King Naresuan (1590–1605). Kicking games such as Chinese cuju are sometimes named as distant relatives. Treat exact origins as tradition rather than settled history.

Adding a net

The net version is modern and Malayan. According to the history in the Wikipedia article on the sport, sepak raga was played over a net on a badminton court in Seremban in 1935. In 1945, Hamid Mydin presented a net game called "sepak raga jaring" in Penang, and the first organised competition followed there that year.

One name, one set of rules

In 1960, officials agreed early rules in Kuala Lumpur and set up a Malayan sepak raga federation. Representatives from Malaya, Singapore, Myanmar and Thailand also met in Kuala Lumpur and settled on a compromise name. "Sepak" is Malay for "kick", and "takraw" comes from Thai and refers to a woven rattan ball. Together the name means roughly "kick the woven ball".

The Asian Sepaktakraw Federation (ASTAF) followed in 1965, and the sport was a medal event at that year's Southeast Asian Peninsular Games in Kuala Lumpur. Thailand began replacing rattan balls with woven synthetic ones in 1982.

Going international

The International Sepaktakraw Federation (ISTAF) was formed in 1988 by Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia and Myanmar. Sepak takraw became a medal sport at the Asian Games in Beijing in 1990, and women's events were added in 1998.

ISTAF launched its World Cup and its SuperSeries circuit in 2011.

How it's played

These rules follow ISTAF's Law of the Game 2024, which has been in force since 1 February 2024. Older guides, and some local events, still use the previous 21-point scoring, explained below.

The court

The court is 13.4 m long and 6.1 m wide, with no obstacles up to 8 m above the floor and a free zone at least 3 m wide all around. A centre line divides the court into two halves, one per team.

At each end of the centre line, a quarter circle with a 0.9 m radius is marked where it meets each side line. In each half there is a service circle with a 0.3 m radius, centred 2.45 m from the back line and 3.05 m from each side line.

The net

The net is 0.7 m deep and stretches across the centre line. Its top is 1.52 m high in the middle for men and 1.42 m for women, rising to 1.55 m and 1.45 m at the posts. That is about badminton height, low enough to make the overhead kicks possible.

Teams and positions

The classic format is the regu: three players a side, plus up to two reserves.

  • Tekong (server): plays at the back and serves from the service circle.
  • Left inside: often called the feeder or setter, who sets the ball up for an attack.
  • Right inside: often called the striker or killer, who spikes the ball over the net.

The two inside players stand in the quarter circles while their team serves. In a team event, each country fields three different regus, and the team that wins two of the three regu matches wins.

ISTAF also has doubles (two players a side) and quadrant (four a side) formats, with team versions of each. In those formats the server stands behind the back line rather than in the service circle.

Serving

The serving side's inside player throws the ball to the tekong, who must kick it straight over the net. The tekong's other foot must stay in the service circle until the kick. Since 2024, serve alternates after every point, whoever wins it.

Scoring

Every fault gives a point to the other side, whether that side was serving or not (rally scoring).

  • A set is won by the first side to 15 points.
  • At 14–14, the referee announces "setting up to 17", and the set goes to the first side to reach 17.
  • A match is best of three sets, with two-minute breaks between sets. Teams change ends at 8 points in the third set.

Which version? These are the ISTAF rules since 1 February 2024. Before that, for about a decade, ISTAF sets went to 21 points, capped at 25 after 20–20, and each side served three times in a row. ISTAF changed it to shorten matches. Some national associations, including Malaysia's, argued for a return to 21 points, but in 2024 ISTAF said the 15-point system would stay.

Touches and faults

Each side may play the ball up to three times in succession before it crosses the net. Common faults include:

  • Touching the ball with the hand or arm.
  • Playing the ball more than three times.
  • Catching or trapping the ball under the arm, between the legs or against the body.
  • Touching the net, the posts or the referee's chair with any part of the body or kit.
  • Crossing into the other court, except in the natural follow-through of a kick or block.
  • Touching the ball on the opponent's side.
  • The ball hitting the ceiling, a wall or any object other than the net.
  • On the serve: inside players moving out of their quarter circles, or the tekong lifting the planted foot before the kick.

The officials

Under the 2024 Law of the Game, each match has a Referee at one end of the net, an Assistant Referee opposite, a Court Referee behind the Referee and two Line Referees along the side lines. An Official Referee supervises from off court.

Players and officials can be shown yellow and red cards. A player sent off may be replaced only if the team still has a substitution left in that set.

Match length

There is no game clock: a match lasts until one side wins two sets. Each regu may call one time-out of up to a minute per set and make two substitutions per set.

Equipment

  • The ball: originally hand-woven rattan. Today's ISTAF ball is a single woven layer of synthetic fibre with 12 holes and 20 crossing points. ISTAF's 2024 rules give 0.41–0.43 m around and 170–180 g for men, and 0.42–0.44 m and 150–160 g for women. Rubber-covered balls are allowed only if ISTAF approves them.
  • The net and posts: a fine nylon net with 6–8 cm mesh, held at 1.55 m (men) or 1.45 m (women) at the posts.
  • Kit: a numbered jersey, shorts, socks and rubber-soled sports shoes without heels. The regu captain wears an armband on the left upper arm.

Where it's played today

ISTAF governs the sport worldwide. Its secretariat is in Singapore, and its membership includes the Asian federation (ASTAF) and the European federation (FESTA). The sport's heartland is Southeast Asia, but there are national teams in South and East Asia, Europe, the Americas and beyond.

Major competitions

  • Asian Games: sepak takraw has been a medal sport since 1990.
  • Southeast Asian (SEA) Games: a medal sport since the 1965 Southeast Asian Peninsular Games.
  • King's Cup: the Takraw Association of Thailand's world championship, held since 1985 and often seen as the most prestigious event.
  • ISTAF World Cup: first held in Kuala Lumpur in 2011.
  • ISTAF SuperSeries: a circuit of tournaments that started in Bangkok in 2011.

Thailand is the dominant power. Malaysia is its great rival, and Myanmar, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea, Japan and India are all medal contenders.

Famous moments and players

Hamid Mydin and the first net game

Hamid Mydin is credited with presenting the net version of sepak raga in Penang in 1945, the step that turned a circle game into a competitive sport. (Sepak takraw - Wikipedia)

Thailand's Asian Games run

Malaysia topped the sepak takraw medal table at the first two Asian Games events, in 1990 and 1994. Thailand topped it at every Games from 1998 to 2022 and has won well over half of all the sport's Asian Games gold medals. (Sepak takraw at the Asian Games - Wikipedia)

Chinlone at the SEA Games

When Myanmar hosted the 2013 SEA Games, chinlone, its traditional circle game, was contested for the first time. Its inclusion was controversial because other countries had little experience of it. (Chinlone - Wikipedia)

India's first World Cup gold

On 25 March 2025, at the Sepak Takraw World Cup in Patna, India's men's regu beat Japan 2–1 in the final (11–15, 15–11, 17–14). It was India's first ever World Cup gold. The final set was decided by the new "setting up to 17" rule. (The Bridge)

pages.title: Netball
pages.content:
What is netball?

Netball is a team ball game for two sides of seven players. You score by throwing the ball through a ring on a tall post, a bit like basketball, but there is no backboard, no dribbling and no running with the ball.

Once you catch the ball you have three seconds to pass or shoot, and you can barely move your feet. Every player also has a fixed position that limits where on the court they may go. That makes netball a game of quick, precise passing and clever movement off the ball.

It is one of the most popular team sports for women and girls in the Commonwealth. Commonly cited figures put it at more than 20 million players in over 80 countries, and men's and mixed netball are growing too.

History and origins

From women's basketball

Netball grew out of basketball, which James Naismith invented in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891. Women began playing the new game almost at once, and teachers soon adapted it for girls and women.

Two adaptations matter for netball. In New Orleans, the teacher Clara Baer asked Naismith for the rules. She is said to have misread lines on his court diagram as zones that players could not leave. Her women's rules, published in 1895, kept players in areas of the court, and World Netball's history says this misreading was written into women's basketball rules by 1899.

In England, Martina Bergman-Österberg introduced a form of basketball to her students in Hampstead, London, in 1893. Her college later moved to Dartford in Kent. According to the Wikipedia history of the sport, the game was moved outdoors there in 1897, played with netted rings, and given the name "net ball".

The two strands are often told together, and sources differ on the exact dates and on how much each teacher shaped the game. What is clear is that zones, a ban on running with the ball and a goal without a backboard were in place very early.

Rules, nations and a world body

The Ling Association in England published the first codified netball rules in 1901 (some accounts say 1900). The game spread through schools across the British Empire, but for decades each country played slightly differently, with seven, nine or even five players a side.

National bodies followed: New Zealand in 1924, the All England Net Ball Association in 1926 and an Australian association in 1927. Australia beat New Zealand 40–11 in the first international match, in Melbourne in 1938.

After an Australian tour of England in the 1950s showed how different the national rules were, representatives from England, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the West Indies met in Sri Lanka in 1960. They agreed one set of seven-a-side rules and founded the International Federation of Women's Basketball and Netball.

That body was later renamed the International Netball Federation, and on 3 June 2021 it rebranded as World Netball.

World Cups and the Commonwealth Games

The first world tournament was held in Eastbourne, England, in 1963, and it has been held about every four years since. Today it is called the Netball World Cup.

The International Olympic Committee recognised netball in 1995. Netball became a medal sport at the Commonwealth Games in Kuala Lumpur in 1998 and has been on the programme ever since. It has never been an Olympic sport.

Netball keeps evolving. World Netball developed a shorter, faster format, first called Fast Net and now FAST5, and in 2022 men played in a World Netball event for the first time, at the men's FAST5 World Series.

How it's played

These rules follow the Rules of Netball, 2024 Edition from World Netball, the current edition. It came into force for international matches on 1 January 2024. National leagues can add their own variations.

The court

The court is a rectangle 30.5 m long and 15.25 m wide (100 by 50 feet). Two lines across it, called transverse lines, divide it into three equal parts: a goal third at each end and a centre third in the middle.

In the middle of the court is a small centre circle, 0.9 m (3 ft) across. At each end is a goal circle, a semicircle with a radius of 4.9 m (16 ft) measured from the middle of the goal line.

The goalpost stands at the middle of each goal line. It is 3.05 m (10 ft) high, with a ring of 380 mm (15 in) inside diameter and a net open at the bottom. There is no backboard.

Seven players and their areas

Each team has seven players on court. Each wears a bib with position initials, and each may only play in certain areas:

  • Goal Shooter (GS): the attacking goal third, including the goal circle.
  • Goal Attack (GA): the centre third and the attacking goal third, including the goal circle.
  • Wing Attack (WA): the centre third and the attacking goal third, but not the goal circle.
  • Centre (C): everywhere except the two goal circles.
  • Wing Defence (WD): the centre third and the defending goal third, but not the goal circle.
  • Goal Defence (GD): the centre third and the defending goal third, including the goal circle.
  • Goal Keeper (GK): the defending goal third, including the goal circle.

Going into an area your position does not allow is called offside. The other team gets a free pass.

Scoring

Only the Goal Shooter and Goal Attack can score, and only from inside the goal circle. A goal counts one point, and the team with more goals at the end wins.

Some professional leagues add a two-point Super Shot. This is a competition rule, not part of World Netball's rules. Suncorp Super Netball in Australia introduced it in 2020: in the last five minutes of each quarter, a goal from a marked zone at the outer edge of the circle counts two. The ANZ Premiership in New Zealand and the Netball Super League in Britain added their own versions in 2025.

The centre pass

Play starts with a centre pass, taken by the Centre standing in the centre circle. It restarts the same way after every goal, and teams take turns no matter who scored.

When the umpire whistles, the other players may move into the centre third. The pass must be caught or touched by a player standing in, or landing in, the centre third.

Key rules

  • Footwork: after catching the ball, a player can pivot or step with the other foot, but must pass or shoot before the landing foot touches the ground again. No running, dragging the foot or hopping.
  • Three seconds: the ball must be passed or shot within three seconds of catching it ("held ball").
  • Obstruction: a defender may try to block or intercept, but must stay at least 0.9 m (3 ft) away from the player with the ball. The distance is measured on the ground from the attacker's landing foot.
  • Contact: no pushing, tripping, holding, knocking the ball out of someone's hands or otherwise interfering with an opponent by contact, whether deliberate or accidental.
  • Over a third: the ball cannot be thrown over a whole third. It must be caught or touched by a player in each third it passes through.
  • Short pass: there must be room for an opponent to intercept between passer and receiver.
  • Replaying: a player who drops the ball or misses a shot cannot be the first to touch it again, unless it has bounced off the post or ring.

The 2024 edition also scrapped the old toss-up, which was used when two players held the ball at the same time.

Fouls and penalties

Minor infringements such as footwork, held ball, offside and over a third give the other team a free pass. A player taking a free pass cannot shoot.

Major infringements, obstruction and contact, give a penalty pass. If it is awarded in the goal circle, the Goal Shooter or Goal Attack can choose to pass or shoot. Until the penalty is taken, the player who caused it must stand beside the thrower and take no part in play.

For repeated or dangerous play, umpires can warn a player, suspend them for two minutes of playing time, or order them off for the rest of the match.

The officials

A match is controlled by two umpires, each in charge of one half of the court and one side line, with a reserve umpire on the bench. Scorers and timekeepers help them.

Match length

A match is four quarters of 15 minutes. There are four-minute breaks after the first and third quarters and a 12-minute half-time (eight minutes if organisers and both teams agree). Teams change ends every quarter. Tournaments can use extra time to settle a tied match.

Equipment

  • Ball: round, made of leather, rubber or a similar synthetic material, 690–710 mm around and 400–450 g.
  • Goalposts: padded metal poles 3.05 m high with a ring and net and no backboard.
  • Bibs: position initials 150 mm high, worn front and back.
  • Clothing: team uniform and sports shoes without spikes. Body piercings, including earrings, may not be worn.
  • Court: preferably a sprung wooden floor, but netball is also played outdoors on hard courts and grass.

Where it's played today

World Netball, based in the Manchester area of England, runs the international game. In April 2025 it had 63 full and 12 associate member nations across five regions: Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania.

The strongest nations come mostly from the Commonwealth: Australia, New Zealand, England, Jamaica and South Africa. Netball is also a major sport in Malawi, elsewhere in Africa and the Caribbean, and in Pacific island nations.

Major competitions

  • Netball World Cup: every four years. The 2027 tournament is planned for Sydney.
  • Commonwealth Games: netball has been a medal sport since 1998.
  • Netball Quad Series: a regular test series between the top nations.
  • FAST5 World Series: the short, high-scoring format.

Professional leagues

  • Suncorp Super Netball in Australia.
  • ANZ Premiership in New Zealand.
  • Netball Super League in Britain (formerly the Superleague, started in 2005).

Many Jamaican, South African, Malawian and English internationals play in these leagues, especially in Australia.

Famous moments and players

Australia's World Cup record

Australia is the most successful team in netball history. By the Wikipedia count of Netball World Cup results, it has won 12 world titles, most recently beating England 61–45 in the 2023 final in Cape Town. (Netball World Cup - Wikipedia)

New Zealand by one goal, 2019

At the 2019 Netball World Cup in Liverpool, the New Zealand Silver Ferns beat Australia 52–51 in the final. It was New Zealand's fifth world title, including one shared in 1979. (Netball World Cup - Wikipedia)

England's last-second gold, 2018

In the Commonwealth Games final on the Gold Coast in April 2018, England trailed hosts Australia by up to four goals in the last quarter. Helen Housby then scored on the final buzzer to win 52–51. It was England's first Commonwealth Games netball gold. (World Netball)

Irene van Dyk

The goal shooter Irene van Dyk played 72 internationals for South Africa (1994–1999) and 145 for New Zealand (2000–2014). That made her the most-capped netball international in the world. She won the 2003 world title with New Zealand. (Irene van Dyk - Wikipedia)

pages.title: Kho kho
pages.content:
What is kho kho?

Kho kho is a fast tag game from India, played by two teams on a rectangular court with a wooden pole at each end.

One team chases and the other defends. Most of the chasers sit or squat in a line down the middle of the court, facing alternate ways. Only one chaser is "active" at a time. To pass the chase on, the active chaser touches a sitting teammate on the back and calls out "kho!" The two swap roles, and the new chaser sets off at once.

The defenders come on in small groups and try to dodge and survive as long as they can. Because chasers can only run in set directions, the game is a mix of sprinting, dodging and teamwork.

The name comes from the Marathi word kho-kho; "kho" imitates the sound players make when passing on the chase.

History and origins

Tradition and early forms

Kho kho is one of India's traditional games, but its early history is hard to pin down. Some writers claim it has been played since at least the 4th century BCE, and some link parts of it to episodes in the Mahabharata. Wikipedia notes that the early-dating claim needs better sources, so these links are best treated as tradition rather than established history.

Tradition also describes an older version called Rathera, said to have been played on chariots (ratha means chariot in Sanskrit).

The modern game

The modern game was organised in 1914, when the Deccan Gymkhana club in Pune gave it formal rules. The first rule book is reportedly linked to the independence leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

Kho kho was shown at the 1936 Berlin Olympics as a demonstration sport, alongside kabaddi. The national body, now the Kho Kho Federation of India (KKFI), was founded in 1955 as the Akhil Bharatiya Kho Kho Mandal, and held its first competition in 1959.

Kho kho was demonstrated at the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi, and became a medal sport at the South Asian Games in 2016. The game was traditionally played on earth; top-level matches now use mats.

How it's played

There are two main formats today. The standard format is the traditional game run by the KKFI at national championships. The fast format, with seven chasers on court, is used by the Ultimate Kho Kho league and was used at the 2025 World Cup. Measurements below are for senior players; junior courts are smaller.

The court

Under the standard rules the court is 27 m long and 16 m wide.

  • A wooden pole stands at each end, 24 m apart. Each pole is 120–125 cm high and 9–10 cm thick, smooth and round.
  • A central lane, 30 cm wide, runs down the middle from pole to pole.
  • Cross lanes, 35 cm wide, cross the central lane at right angles. The chasers sit where they meet. Neighbouring cross lanes are 2.3 m apart.
  • Behind each pole is a free zone, about 1.5 m deep, where the active chaser can move freely and change direction.

The central lane splits the court into two halves. The fast format uses a shorter court, 22 m by 16 m, and chasers squat in marked 40 cm squares.

Teams

In the standard game a squad has up to 15 players, 12 are named for a match, and nine take the field. When chasing, eight sit in the central lane and one is the active chaser. When defending, players come on in batches of three. When all three in a batch are out, the next batch must come in straight away.

In the fast format, seven chasers are on court.

Sitting chasers and the "kho"

The sitting chasers face alternate sides of the court: one faces left, the next faces right, and so on. They must not get up or move until they get a kho.

To give a valid kho, the active chaser:

  1. comes up behind a sitting teammate,
  2. touches them on the back (between the shoulders and the waist),
  3. and says "kho" clearly.

The kho must be given before the active chaser passes the cross lane of the player they mean to touch. The new chaser then gets up and runs; the old one sits down in the empty spot.

Direction rules

These rules are what make kho kho tricky:

  • A new chaser may only go into the half of the court they were facing while sitting.
  • Once a chaser has set off towards one pole, they must keep going that way. Going back over ground already covered is called receding and is a foul.
  • The active chaser may not cross the central lane into the other half. To change halves or direction, they must run round a pole through the free zone, or pass the chase on with a kho.

If a chaser breaks a rule, the umpire calls a foul. Until it is cleared, the chasers cannot get anyone out. The chaser clears it by turning away and running the other way until they give a kho or reach a free zone.

Dives

Diving is one of the most exciting parts of the game:

  • In a pole dive, the chaser holds a pole with one hand and stretches out to tag a defender with the other.
  • In a sky dive, the chaser leaps through the air to tag a defender who is just out of reach.

Some direction rules are relaxed during a pole dive, but touching or crossing the central lane is still a foul.

Scoring

A defender is out, and the chasers score, when:

  • the active chaser tags them fairly with a hand,
  • they step completely out of the court,
  • or they are late coming on with a new batch.

In the standard game each out is worth one point. In the fast format each tag is worth two points, and a batch of defenders that survives at least three minutes earns a Dream Run bonus point for the defending side, plus a point for each extra 30 seconds.

The fast format also has a wazir: one chaser who may change direction. During a powerplay, the chasing team can have two wazirs until the current batch of defenders is out.

Officials

A senior match is run by a referee, two umpires, a timekeeper and a scorer, usually with an assistant scorer. The umpires call fouls with the whistle.

Match length

A standard match has two innings. In each innings, each team chases for one turn and defends for one turn. A senior turn lasts 9 minutes, with short breaks between turns and a longer break between innings.

In the fast format each turn is 7 minutes. If a match is level, a minimum chase is used: each team gets one extra turn, and the first to score wins.

Equipment

Kho kho needs very little:

  • Two smooth wooden poles fixed at the ends of the court.
  • A marked court, either earth or, at top level, mats.
  • Light shoes and a sports kit with numbers.

There is no ball. Wikipedia notes that playing on mats takes more energy than playing on earth and may lead to more injuries.

Where it's played today

Governing bodies

  • The Kho Kho Federation of India (KKFI) runs the sport in India. It holds national championships every year for men, women and juniors.
  • The International Kho Kho Federation (IKKF) was founded in 2018 and is based in New Delhi. It wants to spread the game to enough countries to be considered for the Olympics.
  • The Asian Kho Kho Federation runs the Asian Championship. India won the 4th edition in 2023.

Ultimate Kho Kho

Ultimate Kho Kho (UKK) is a professional franchise league run with the KKFI. It started in 2022 with six teams and uses the seven-a-side fast format, with seven-minute turns.

The first season ran from 14 August to 4 September 2022 and was broadcast by Sony. Odisha Juggernauts won the first final 46–45 against Telugu Yoddhas. Gujarat Giants won the 2023–24 season, beating Chennai Quick Guns 31–26.

The first Kho Kho World Cup (2025)

The first Kho Kho World Cup was held at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in New Delhi from 13 to 19 January 2025, organised by the KKFI and the IKKF. It used the fast seven-a-side format.

Reports differ on the number of countries: news reports at the opening said 20, while Wikipedia lists 23 countries, with 20 men's and 19 women's teams.

India won both titles, unbeaten, beating Nepal in both finals:

  • Women: India 78–40 Nepal.
  • Men: India 54–36 Nepal.

Famous moments and players

  • Priyanka Ingle. The Pune player captained India's women to the 2025 World Cup title and was named best player of the tournament. She won the Rani Laxmibai Award in 2022. (Source: Wikipedia.)
  • Chaithra B's Dream Run (2025). In the last turn of the women's World Cup final, Chaithra B's batch of defenders stayed in for 5 minutes 14 seconds, earning Dream Run points that closed out India's win. (Source: The Bridge; Wikipedia.)
  • Pratik Waikar. He captained India's men to the 2025 World Cup title. (Source: The Bridge.)
  • Ramji Kashyap. He was named Player of the Season in both of the first two Ultimate Kho Kho seasons. (Source: Wikipedia, Ultimate Kho Kho.)
  • Odisha Juggernauts' one-point title (2022). The first Ultimate Kho Kho final was decided 46–45. (Source: Wikipedia, Ultimate Kho Kho.)

pages.title: Floorball
pages.content:
What is floorball?

Floorball is an indoor team sport played with light sticks and a hollow plastic ball. It looks a little like ice hockey, but it is played in shoes on a hard floor. Body checking is not allowed, and the stick must stay low.

Each team has five field players and a goalkeeper on the rink. The goalkeeper plays without a stick. The aim is simple: score more goals than the other team.

The game is fast and cheap to start. All you need is a stick, a ball, a gym and some goals. That has helped it spread from schools and clubs to a professional top level in northern Europe.

The sport has different names in different countries. Swedes call it innebandy ("indoor bandy") and Finns call it salibandy ("hall bandy"). In Switzerland it is unihockey.

History and origins

Gym-hall roots

People have played stick-and-ball games indoors for a long time. Plastic floor-hockey sticks and balls were used in many US school gyms in the 1950s and 1960s.

Floorball as we know it took shape in Sweden from the late 1960s and through the 1970s. Sources disagree on exact dates and on which club came first.

Wikipedia says basic rules were set in Sweden in 1979, and official match rules were first written down in 1981. Sweden's national association joined the IFF's list of members with a founding date of 7 November 1981.

An international federation

The International Floorball Federation (IFF) was founded on 12 April 1986 in Huskvarna, Sweden. Its three founders were the national associations of Sweden, Finland and Switzerland. The IFF is now based in Helsinki. As of 2024 it had 81 member associations.

The IFF's first big event was the European Cup in 1993. That club competition is now called the Champions Cup.

  • Men's World Championships: first held in 1996 in Stockholm. Sweden beat Finland 5–0 in the final.
  • Women's World Championships: first held in 1997 in Mariehamn, Finland. Sweden beat Finland 4–2 in the final.

The International Olympic Committee recognised the IFF in December 2008. In July 2011 it welcomed the IFF as a Recognised International Sports Federation. Floorball is not an Olympic sport.

How it's played

The rules here follow the IFF Rules of the Game, 2026 edition, in force from 1 July 2026. The IFF published this edition in February 2026, and it replaced the 2022 edition. Most of the basics below are the same in both editions.

The rink

  • Size: a standard rink is 40 m × 20 m (smallest allowed: 36 m × 18 m). It is surrounded by IFF-approved boards with rounded corners, about 50 cm high.
  • Centre line and centre spot: split the rink into two halves. Each period starts with a face-off at the centre spot.
  • Goal crease: a 4 m × 5 m rectangle in front of each goal, marked 2.85 m from the end boards. This is the goalkeeper's working area.
  • Goalkeeper area: a small 1 m × 2.5 m rectangle inside the crease. Field players may not enter it.
  • Goal line: the back line of the goalkeeper area. Goal posts stand on it, 1.6 m apart.
  • Goals: IFF-approved goal cages, 160 cm wide and 115 cm high.
  • Face-off dots: on the centre line, and in the corners on the goal-line extensions, 1.5 m from the side boards.

Teams and substitutions

A team may list up to 20 players. At most six may be on the rink at once: five field players plus a goalkeeper, or six field players with no goalkeeper.

Substitutions are unlimited and on the fly, through the team's own substitution zone. Players usually play short, intense shifts.

Positions

The rules only name two roles: goalkeepers and field players. Teams usually have two or three lines of five field players, and they change whole lines at a time.

Goalkeepers stop shots with their hands and body. Inside the crease they may catch the ball and throw it. If the throw goes over the centre line, it must first touch the floor, a board or a player. They may hold the ball for no more than 3 seconds.

Goalkeepers may not take a deliberate pass from a team-mate with their hands. If a goalkeeper leaves the crease completely, they count as a field player without a stick.

Scoring

A goal is scored when the whole ball crosses the goal line from the front, played correctly. You may not kick the ball in on purpose or direct it in with your body.

A face-off, hit-in or free-hit can go straight into the goal.

Key rules on the stick and body

  • Ball below the knee: You may not play, or try to play, the ball above knee level with your stick, foot or lower leg. Stopping the ball with your thigh is allowed.
  • No high sticks: Your blade may not go above waist level in your back-swing or follow-through when other players are near.
  • No hitting the stick: You may not hit, block, lift or kick an opponent's stick.
  • No checking: Only shoulder-to-shoulder contact is allowed. You may not push, hold or trip opponents, or back into them.
  • No sticks between the legs: You may not put your stick, foot or leg between an opponent's legs or feet.
  • Stay on your feet: You may not jump to stop the ball, or play it with your head.
  • No hands: Field players may not play the ball with a hand or arm. Playing it while lying on the floor to gain an advantage is also a foul.

Free-hits and other restarts

Most fouls lead to a free-hit for the other team, taken where the foul happened. Opponents must stand at least 3 m away, sticks included.

The ball must be hit, not dragged or flicked. A free-hit is never taken closer than 3.5 m to the goalkeeper area. If the fouled team still has the ball, the referees play advantage.

When the ball goes over the boards, the other team takes a hit-in, 1.5 m from the boards. A face-off restarts play when no team can be given the ball.

Penalties

Serious fouls send a player to the penalty bench, so the team plays short-handed. The 2022 rules changed the old system: the 5-minute penalty was replaced by a "2+2" major penalty. The 2026 rules keep this structure.

  • Minor bench penalty: 2 minutes. For example, for slashing at an opponent's stick to win a big advantage, playing the ball above the waist, careless stick or body play, a hand ball, too many players on the rink, or protesting.
  • Major bench penalty: 2 + 2 minutes. For reckless play with the stick, hooking an opponent's body with the stick, throwing a stick at the ball, or reckless physical play.
  • 10-minute personal penalty: For unsporting behaviour or diving. The player sits out, but the team can replace them on the rink. It always comes with a bench penalty.
  • Technical match penalty: Sends a player off for the rest of the match, for technical offences such as using a non-approved stick.
  • Match penalty: Sends a player off for the rest of the match and the next match, and may lead to more punishment. It covers violent or brutal play, fights and gross misconduct.

If the opponents score during a bench penalty, the penalty usually ends early.

Penalty shots

A penalty shot is given when a foul stops a clear goal-scoring situation. The shooter starts with the stick from a spot 5 m from the centre line, midway across the rink, and goes one-on-one with the goalkeeper. Every other player waits in the substitution zone.

Officials

A match is led by two referees with equal authority. A neutral match secretariat keeps the match record, runs the clock and makes announcements.

Match length

  • Regular time: 3 × 20 minutes of effective time (the clock stops at every whistle), with two 10-minute breaks. Organisers may allow shorter games, but not shorter than 2 × 15 minutes.
  • Time out: each team gets one, lasting 30 seconds.
  • Overtime: if a match must have a winner, there is 10 minutes of sudden-death overtime, then penalty shots, five per team to start.

Equipment

  • Stick: a shaft, usually carbon fibre, with a plastic blade. It must be IFF-approved and marked. The blade may not be sharp, and its hook may not exceed 30 mm. Wikipedia gives the usual limits as at most 114 cm long and 350 g.
  • Ball: IFF-approved hollow plastic, single-coloured, 72 mm across, about 23 g, with 26 holes. Shots have been recorded at around 200 km/h.
  • Goalkeeper: must wear an IFF-approved face mask, a jersey and long trousers. Padding must fit the body and must not be shaped to cover the goal.
  • Players: jersey, shorts, socks and indoor shoes. Jewellery is banned. The IFF advises national associations to make protective goggles compulsory for under-17s.

Where it's played today

The IFF governs floorball worldwide. National associations run their own leagues and cups, such as Czechia's Superliga (pictured below).

The four leading nations are Sweden, Finland, Switzerland and Czechia. Sweden and Finland have won every men's world title.

Major competitions:

  • Men's World Floorball Championships: every two years, in even-numbered years. Sweden has 10 titles and Finland 5. The 2026 edition is in Tampere, Finland.
  • Women's World Floorball Championships: every two years, in odd-numbered years. Sweden has 11 titles, Finland 2 and Switzerland 2.
  • U19 World Championships for young players.
  • Champions Cup: the top club tournament for the best men's and women's clubs. It began as the European Cup in 1993.
  • The World Games: floorball has been played at the multi-sport World Games, most recently in Chengdu, China, in 2025.

Famous moments and players

  • Finland end Sweden's run (2008): In the men's world final in Prague, Finland beat Sweden 7–6 in overtime. It was Finland's first world title. It ended Sweden's six straight titles and was the first world championship game Sweden had ever lost. Source: 2008 Men's World Floorball Championships - Wikipedia.
  • Overtime in Malmö (2024): Finland beat hosts Sweden 5–4 in overtime in the men's world final. Source: Men's World Floorball Championship - Wikipedia.
  • Switzerland's women (2025): In Ostrava, Switzerland beat the Czech Republic 2–0 to win their second world title. A record 8,844 spectators watched the final. Source: 2025 Women's World Floorball Championships - Wikipedia.
  • Mika Kohonen (Finland): Played in 11 men's World Championships from 1998 to 2018 and won a medal at every one, including four golds. He was voted the world's best player a record five times in the Innebandymagazinet poll. He entered the IFF Hall of Fame in 2021. Source: Mika Kohonen - Wikipedia.
